\Section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A roadblock to the adoption of program verification is the \emph{cost of specification}.
The properties developers care about are high-level --- a call chain aborts only under stated preconditions, an entrypoint satisfies its postconditions, stored data respects an invariant --- but to prove any of them, the supporting functions need contracts of their own, and those are often boilerplate, as they restate what the code does.
\emph{Specification inference} derives such contracts from the program, so that effort can go to the properties worth stating by hand.
The classical engine for mechanical inference is Dijkstra's weakest-precondition transformation (\WP)~\cite{dijkstra1975wp}: propagated backward through a function, it yields the exact abort condition and the exact postcondition. However, it depends on loop invariants to provide an induction hypothesis~\cite{BL05}, and despite a long history of research~\cite{CousotHalbwachs78}, there is no complete technique for synthesizing them.

This paper describes a novel combination of agentic specification inference, as studied, e.g., in~\cite{VeriStruct26,MSG25}, and weakest-precondition transformation.
The agent conducts the inference, supplies loop invariants, and calls \WP and the verifier as tools.
The approach is implemented for the Move smart contract language, which is similar to Rust. Move has strong verification support through the Move Prover (\MVP)~\cite{DillGPQXZ22,GrieskampEtAl26HO}.
Move shares its reference semantics with safe Rust and is therefore amenable to reference elimination, which the Move Prover has applied since its beginning~\cite{DillGPQXZ22}.
On reference-eliminated Move bytecode, we run classical \WP and map Move's references into the predicate calculus of the specification language.
Moreover, \emph{behavioral predicates}~\cite{GrieskampEtAl26HO}, which let a specification refer to the contract of another function as a black box, make \WP fully modular.

We evaluate the combination on a corpus of 26 inference problems.
Twenty-four of them are extracted from public Move code of the Aptos framework that has no specification: a model may have seen the code during training, but it cannot recall a specification that was never written.
We compare three tactics, one without the \WP tool and two with it, under two models of one family, the frontier model Sol~5.6 and the mid-tier model Terra~5.6, and check completeness with withheld mutants.
Without the \WP tool, the agent already does well: it completes 99\% of its cells under the frontier model and 93\% under the mid-tier model.
With \WP, completeness does not change measurably, but the cost drops by 11--21\%.
The saving comes from the targets without loops, where \WP derives the complete contract and the hybrid tactics cost 36--60\% of the agent alone; on loop targets, where the agent still has to find the invariant, they cost 9--22\% more.
The mid-tier model costs 53--59\% of the frontier model, close to the ratio of their prices, and falls behind it mainly on the one target whose contract needs a permutation argument proved with lemmas.

\Paragraph{Contributions}
The paper presents a novel combination of agentic and mechanical specification inference, integrated with the Move Prover, and a detailed empirical evaluation on real-world code, which shows that such a combination lowers the cost of specification inference where the mechanical analysis applies.
In addition, we show that reference elimination in the style of the Move Prover is a good basis for specification inference.

The Move Prover was developed for the Diem project and has \Anon{been maintained by Aptos Labs since 2022}{since been maintained by a blockchain company}; it has verified Diem's payment system and critical components of \Anon{the Aptos blockchain}{a public blockchain}~\cite{ParkZGXGCLC24,AptosFrameworkBook}.
